intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The note under each slide explains it, gives you something to remember and warns where people slip. Work each worked example in pencil first, then close the page and answer the recall questions from memory before you check the deck.

sections.title: Why the shape of the money matters
sections.big_idea: A finance headline is a construct. Ask what it counts, because **the instrument decides what the money does**, and headline size hides it.
in_plain_words: Developed countries reported US$115.9 billion of climate finance for 2022, and Oxfam and CARE put the real value at US$28 to 35 billion from the same reporting. Neither is a mistake. A loan is reported at face value, so ten million lent counts like ten million given. Netting out repayment and interest cuts the headline sharply.

That is why four words need exact definitions: development finance, concessionality, mobilisation and de-risking. The system has also moved from lending to states towards making projects investible for private capital. Three questions help: **who bears the risk, who repays and when, and what was given up to get it**.

right.title: Assessed, 2022
items: Grant equivalent of the same flows

diagram.caption: one set of flows, two questions

key_terms.meaning: Public or publicly backed money on better terms than a commercial lender offers.
How much better than market terms a loan is, shown as a grant element.
Private capital a public intervention is claimed to have caused to flow.
The public side absorbing risks that private investors will not carry.
A guarantee-type obligation that costs nothing until it is called.

worked_example.title: Compute a grant element
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A loan has a face value of US$100 million, and the present value of its repayments is US$40 million. The grant element is face value minus that present value, shown as a percentage of face value.
steps: Value given as a gift: 100 − 40 = 60 million.
Grant element: 60 ÷ 100 = 60%.
A pure grant has a grant element of 100% and a loan at the discount rate has zero.
Counting this loan at its US$100 million face value would report more than it delivers.
worked_example.answer: The grant element is 60 per cent, so the loan delivers well under its headline.

mistakes: Comparing two finance figures without asking what each one counts.
Judging a loan by its headline size instead of its concessionality.
Treating a guarantee as free because no cash moves on signing.

recall.q: What gap opens Module One?
recall.a: US$115.9 billion reported against US$28 to 35 billion assessed for 2022.

recall.q: What does a grant have as a grant element?
recall.a: 100 per cent, by definition.

recall.q: Why is the word caused central to mobilisation?
recall.a: Capital that would have come anyway is only accompanied, and counts for nothing as mobilised.

recall.q: Name the three questions to ask of any finance announcement.
recall.a: Who bears the risk, who repays and when, and what was given up to get it.

recall.q: Which period does the fourth row of the history table cover?
recall.a: 2015 to the present, mobilising private capital.

sections.title: The institutions and who decides
sections.big_idea: Lenders differ by owner, borrower and instrument, and **the private arms differ most**, because their borrowers and complaint routes differ.
in_plain_words: Multilateral banks are owned by member states, bilateral agencies by one state, national development banks by their own state, and private arms such as IFC and MIGA lend to firms. Voting at the IBRD follows capital subscription with a small equal allocation of basic votes. IDA gives the poorest countries grants or long-grace credits, so graduating to IBRD is a fiscal event.

Studies of conditionality found reform largely presentational. Woods argues outcomes come from staff, the board and domestic coalitions together. The Articles bar interference in political affairs, which is why **safeguards read as technical standards**. A campaign aimed only at the lender hits one of three actors.

children.label: Private arms and funds
items: IFC and MIGA lend to firms

diagram.caption: who owns the lender decides who can complain

key_terms.meaning: A multilateral development bank, owned by its member states.
The World Bank lender that charges near-market terms to middle-income countries.
The concessional arm for the poorest countries, funded by donor replenishments.
Conditions attached to a loan or programme, such as policy reforms.
A small allocation of votes given equally to all IBRD members.

worked_example.title: Sort four borrowers
worked_example.setup: Illustrative cases. Name the type of lender and who the borrower is in each case.
steps: A state government borrows from the IBRD: a multilateral bank, with a sovereign borrower.
A power company takes a loan from IFC: a private arm, with a firm as borrower and a different complaint body.
A city borrows from JICA: a bilateral agency owned by one state.
A ministry gets a grant from the Green Climate Fund: a climate fund, which lends through accredited entities.
worked_example.answer: Multilateral, private arm, bilateral and climate fund, and only the private arm changes the borrower to a firm.

mistakes: Assuming one country has one vote at the IBRD. Votes follow subscription.
Aiming a campaign at the lender when the domestic coalition is the binding constraint.
Treating IDA and IBRD lending as the same bank on the same terms.

recall.q: Who owns an MDB?
recall.a: Its member states, by subscription.

recall.q: Why does the private-arm row matter most for accountability?
recall.a: The borrower is a company, the safeguard regime differs and the complaint mechanism is a different body.

recall.q: What did Kentikelenis, Stubbs and King find?
recall.a: The reform of IMF conditionality was largely presentational, since the count changed more than the substantive reach.

recall.q: What does graduation from IDA to IBRD change?
recall.a: The terms move from highly concessional to near-market, which is a large event for public finances.

recall.q: Name the three things that produce outcomes in Woods's account.
recall.a: The professional norms of staff, the voting arithmetic of the board and domestic coalitions in the borrower.

sections.title: Instruments: what a loan actually is
sections.big_idea: The instrument decides **who bears the risk**, and the six terms of a loan, especially currency, decide its real burden.
in_plain_words: Sovereign loans, equity, guarantees, political risk insurance and results-based finance put different parties on the hook at different times. Read a loan through its principal, interest, maturity, grace, fees and currency. A grace period flatters early years, and a hard-currency loan serviced from rupee revenue leaves the exchange risk with the borrower.

Guarantees are unpriced public risk with a delayed and correlated cost. Concessionality depends on a chosen discount rate. Debt sustainability analysis is a projection shaped by its assumptions. **The concession agreement is the hard document to get**, and it is where risk allocation lives.

parts.hint: the gift part of the loan

diagram.note: divide by face value to get the grant element, a percentage

key_terms.meaning: Years before principal repayment begins.
The total life of the loan.
The gift share of a loan after repayments are discounted to present value.
Money paid on verified results, with the borrower on the hook until then.
A projection of whether a country can service its debts.

worked_example.title: A currency move
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A project earns rupees and services a dollar loan. Its debt service costs Rs 500 crore a year, and its revenue is Rs 550 crore. The exchange rate then moves by twenty per cent against the borrower.
steps: Extra rupees needed: 500 × 20 ÷ 100 = 100 crore.
New debt service: 500 + 100 = 600 crore.
Revenue of Rs 550 crore now falls short by 600 − 550 = 50 crore.
No term of the loan agreement changed.
worked_example.answer: Debt service rises to Rs 600 crore and the project is Rs 50 crore short, with no clause altered.

mistakes: Treating a sovereign loan and a guarantee as the same thing.
Reading only the first five years of debt service, when the peak may fall on a later administration.
Leaving contingent liabilities out of a sustainability analysis because they are hard to quantify.

recall.q: Which six terms decide a loan's real burden?
recall.a: Principal, interest, maturity, grace period, fees and currency.

recall.q: Which party is on the hook for a guarantee, and when?
recall.a: The guarantor, only if called, on default or a trigger.

recall.q: How does a higher discount rate affect measured concessionality?
recall.a: It raises it, which is why generous rates inflate reported concessional finance.

recall.q: What are the three lending types compared in the table?
recall.a: Investment lending, policy-based lending and results-based lending.

recall.q: Which document is hardest to obtain and why does it matter?
recall.a: The concession agreement, because risk allocation lives there.

sections.title: From lending to de-risking
sections.big_idea: The 2015 turn asks public money to **make projects investible** for private capital, and the testable claim is how much it mobilises.
in_plain_words: The MDBs and the IMF argued before 2015 that the SDGs needed far more than aid could supply, so public money should mobilise private capital at a multiple. The Cascade puts public financing last. Gabor reads the agenda as the state absorbing demand and political risk, which contracts away policy space. The documents are public and the direction of travel is documented.

What is open is whether it works. The OECD publishes mobilisation data. Two questions apply to any ratio: **additionality**, whether the investment would have happened anyway, and attribution, who gets credit when several instruments precede one investment. Mobilised money flows mostly to middle-income countries and to sectors with revenue.

diagram.caption: the Cascade, as the World Bank states it

key_terms.meaning: The decision sequence that tests private finance before public money.
Private capital mobilised for each unit of public money.
Whether the private investment would have happened without the public one.
The rule that assigns credit for a private investment among instruments.
Concessional public money mixed with commercial capital in one structure.

worked_example.title: Test a mobilisation claim
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A public guarantee of US$10 million sits beside a private investment of US$50 million. The sponsor claims the guarantee mobilised all of it.
steps: Claimed ratio: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 private dollars per public dollar.
Ask the additionality question: would the investment have happened anyway?
If yes, the guarantee mobilised nothing and only accompanied the deal, so the true ratio is 0.
Ask the attribution question: did a reform or a concessional tranche also help, and by what rule is credit split?
worked_example.answer: The claimed ratio is 5, but it holds only if the investment would not have happened anyway.

mistakes: Quoting a mobilisation total without naming the attribution convention that produced it.
Assuming the critique and the defence disagree about facts. They disagree about the counterfactual.
Applying one conclusion to all countries when mobilisation lands mostly in middle-income ones.

recall.q: What does the Cascade put last?
recall.a: Public financing, after commercial finance and reform options.

recall.q: Who publishes the annual mobilisation data?
recall.a: The OECD.

recall.q: What is the hardest and most important question the module raises?
recall.a: Additionality.

recall.q: Why does the mechanism work least where need is greatest?
recall.a: Private capital needs a return, and poorer markets and social sectors often have none.

recall.q: Name two disclosure questions for blended finance.
recall.a: Are the concessional tranche terms public, and is the mobilisation claim independently checkable.

sections.title: How a project gets financed
sections.big_idea: Project finance lends against a project's own cash flows, so **every risk is allocated by contract**, and the signatory may be a thin SPV.
in_plain_words: Corporate lenders look at a company's whole balance sheet. Project lenders look at the cash flows of a single project, usually held in a special purpose vehicle, and the sponsor's exposure is capped at its equity. Contract, and not corporate reputation, then decides who answers for harm. Affected people are the only party with no contract.

Risk allocation is the whole document: construction, delay, demand, currency, interest rate, change in law and force majeure each have a holder and a clause. Availability payments and take-or-pay move demand risk to the public side. **The financial model's assumptions are the public-interest question**, and renegotiation is normal.

diagram.caption: the cast of a typical financed project

key_terms.meaning: A special purpose vehicle, the company that holds one project.
Lending repaid only from the project's own cash flows.
The offtaker pays for a contracted quantity whether or not it takes delivery.
Payment for keeping an asset available, whatever its use.
A term requiring compensation if a change in law affects returns.

worked_example.title: What take-or-pay costs
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. An offtaker contracts to buy 100 units at Rs 5 a unit under a take-or-pay clause, and takes delivery of only 60.
steps: It pays for the contracted quantity: 100 × 5 = 500.
The value of what it actually took: 60 × 5 = 300.
The payment for unused output is 500 − 300 = 200.
The investor's revenue is near-certain and the demand risk sits with the buyer.
worked_example.answer: The offtaker pays Rs 500, of which Rs 200 buys output it never took.

mistakes: Naming the well-known sponsor as the respondent when the SPV is the legal counterparty.
Asking for the whole financial model when its key assumptions are enough.
Treating renegotiation as a scandal, when it is the normal case over decades.

recall.q: What does a lender look to in project finance?
recall.a: The project's own cash flows.

recall.q: Which party in the cast has no contract?
recall.a: Affected people.

recall.q: Which row of the risk table is most consequential for public policy?
recall.a: Political and regulatory change, through change-in-law and stabilisation clauses.

recall.q: Name two things to ask about a demand forecast.
recall.a: Who produced and paid for it, and the outturn of the same forecaster's last three projects.

recall.q: In what order should you read the documents for a real project?
recall.a: Appraisal, concession agreement, environmental and social assessment, procurement award, implementation report.

sections.title: India's own financing institutions
sections.big_idea: India has tried budget works, PPPs, a development bank and asset sales, and **each disappointment was about execution**: forecasting, risk allocation and renegotiation.
in_plain_words: NaBFID, set up by a 2021 Act, revives the development financial institution for infrastructure after the 1990s and 2000s wind-down. It has authorised capital of Rs 1,00,000 crore and a mandate to develop bond and derivatives markets. The National Monetisation Pipeline identified Rs 6 lakh crore of potential by leasing existing assets.

Viability gap funding is defensible when competitively bid and not stacked on guarantees. The Kelkar Committee diagnosed contracts drafted around fiscal transfer and asked for a renegotiation mechanism. For Indian project information, use ministry sites, PRS, CAG reports, parliamentary answers and clearance portals. **Valuation, and its discount rate, is the whole question in monetisation.**

events.what: DFIs wound down for banks and markets
Kelkar reports to the Finance Minister
NMP Volumes I and II published

key_terms.meaning: The fifth All India Financial Institution, for long-term infrastructure lending.
Transferring the right to operate and collect revenue while ownership stays public.
A capital grant that makes a marginal PPP project viable.
An asset already built, which carries no construction risk.
The 2015 committee that urged designed-in renegotiation for PPPs.

worked_example.title: Two quick checks
worked_example.setup: Check two figures on the slides against each other.
steps: NaBFID shares: 10,000 crore shares × Rs 10 each, so 10,000 × 10 = 1,00,000 crore rupees of authorised capital.
Monetisation: realised about Rs 3.85 lakh crore against a potential of Rs 6 lakh crore, so 3.85 ÷ 6 = 64%.
Note the realisation figure covers three years, while the pipeline covers FY2021-22 to FY2024-25.
worked_example.answer: Authorised capital is Rs 1,00,000 crore, and about 64 per cent of the pipeline had been realised.

mistakes: Calling monetisation privatisation. Ownership is retained and the operating right is leased.
Judging NaBFID on lending volume alone, when it also has a market-development mandate.
Accepting a VGF subsidy without asking whether the gap was bid or negotiated and whose forecast set it.

recall.q: When was the NaBFID Act assented?
recall.a: 28 March 2021.

recall.q: What is the authorised share capital of NaBFID?
recall.a: Rs 1,00,000 crore, in 10,000 crore shares of Rs 10 each.

recall.q: What was the monetisation potential in the pipeline?
recall.a: Rs 6 lakh crore over FY2021-22 to FY2024-25.

recall.q: When is viability gap funding defensible?
recall.a: When competitively bid, capped and disclosed, with the social return above the private return.

recall.q: Which sources are underused for Indian project information?
recall.a: Parliamentary and assembly answers, and CAG reports.

sections.title: Land, environment and consent
sections.big_idea: Two statutes force a project to **describe its own social and environmental cost** in documents you can check against the ground.
in_plain_words: The 2013 land Act replaced the 1894 Act with a social impact assessment, consent for certain acquisitions and statutory resettlement entitlements. Its affected families include the landless, the provision most often under-implemented. The EIA Notification of 2006 runs screening, scoping, public consultation, appraisal and clearance, and category A projects are appraised centrally while category B go to the state.

Clearance conditions are enforceable, and compliance with them is the most tractable challenge. Statutory consent is a procedural threshold and differs from free, prior and informed consent. **Disputes cluster at the exemptions**: category boundaries, expansions, urgency provisions and project splitting.

diagram.caption: the shift is procedural as much as substantive

key_terms.meaning: A statutory step that identifies affected families and checks the need for acquisition.
Rehabilitation and resettlement entitlements set by the Act.
EIA categories that decide whether appraisal is central or at state level.
Enforceable terms on which a project was permitted.
Appraising one development as several smaller projects to stay under a threshold.

worked_example.title: Spot project splitting
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A single development of 120 units is appraised as three projects of 40 units each. Suppose the threshold that triggers fuller appraisal is 100 units.
steps: Add the parts: 3 × 40 = 120 units in all.
Each part is 40 units, below the illustrative threshold of 100.
Taken as a whole, 120 units cross it.
That is the splitting the slide describes, so ask which parts are one project in fact.
worked_example.answer: Each part passes below the threshold that the whole of 120 units would cross.

mistakes: Treating statutory consent as the same standard as free, prior and informed consent.
Challenging the project itself when compliance with its own clearance conditions is the easier route.
Counting only landowners when listing affected families. The Act includes dependants on the land.

recall.q: Which two statutes govern what a financed project owes people on the site?
recall.a: The 2013 land acquisition Act and the EIA Notification of 2006.

recall.q: Who appraises category A projects?
recall.a: The centre. Category B projects are appraised at state level.

recall.q: What do the EIA hearing minutes record?
recall.a: Objections, which are on file whether or not they are accepted.

recall.q: Why is the survey central to consent disputes?
recall.a: It decides who counts as affected, and so the denominator and who has a say.

recall.q: Which provision is most often under-implemented?
recall.a: Entitlements for affected families who hold no title, such as the landless.

sections.title: Climate finance and its accounting
sections.big_idea: The gap in climate finance totals comes from **conventions that all push the number up**, with no falsification needed.
in_plain_words: Five common choices raise the headline: counting loans at face value, using a generous discount rate, counting the full value of partly climate projects, adding mobilised private money and counting finance that would have flowed anyway. Each is defensible and each moves the total in the same direction.

Adequacy, direction and predictability are separate questions. Adaptation is structurally underfunded because it produces avoided loss and no cash flow, so it relies on grants. Loss and damage is contested because it implies responsibility. **Name the specific practice** before alleging greenwashing, and run any claim through four questions: year, instrument, source and method.

key_terms.meaning: Whether the total is large enough against the estimated need.
Where the money goes and as what: adaptation or mitigation, grant or loan.
Harm that has occurred and cannot be adapted to.
The same flow reported by more than one party.
Widening what qualifies so totals rise without flows changing.

worked_example.title: Size the headline gap
worked_example.setup: Use the figures from Module One: US$115.9 billion reported, against US$28 to 35 billion assessed.
steps: Gap at the high assessment: 115.9 − 35 = 80.9 billion.
Gap at the low assessment: 115.9 − 28 = 87.9 billion.
Ratio to the high assessment: 115.9 ÷ 35 = 3.3.
This matches the slide's factor of about three, from face value against grant equivalent.
worked_example.answer: The reported total is about three times the highest assessed figure, a gap of roughly US$81 to 88 billion.

mistakes: Reading the OECD series and the shadow report in the wrong order. Start with the treaty body's assessment.
Calling something greenwashing without naming which practice is alleged.
Using the checklist only against sources you already doubt.

recall.q: Name the five accounting choices that raise the headline.
recall.a: Loans at face value, generous discount rate, full value of partial projects, mobilised private finance added, and finance that would have flowed anyway.

recall.q: Why is adaptation underfunded?
recall.a: It yields avoided losses and no income, so private capital sees no return.

recall.q: Why is loss and damage contested?
recall.a: It is closer to compensation, which implies responsibility.

recall.q: What are the four checklist questions?
recall.a: What year, grant or loan, whose money, and counted how.

recall.q: How long does climate finance reporting lag?
recall.a: Two to three years.

sections.title: Accountability: who can complain
sections.big_idea: Accountability mechanisms judge **the lender against its own rules**, so the first task is naming the financier of the component that caused harm.
in_plain_words: The World Bank's Inspection Panel began in 1994 and has been copied at more than twenty institutions. These mechanisms can investigate compliance, publish findings and require an action plan. They cannot compensate, halt a project directly or bind the borrower government. Jurisdiction follows the financier, and large projects may have several.

Most eligible complaints are never filed, because of practical barriers: unknown financiers, English documents, time limits and fear of retaliation. Intermediaries close that gap. In India, **the domestic forums carry the remedies and the lender mechanism carries the record**. Read case files end to end, including ones the mechanism declined.

diagram.caption: the practical sequence for a complaint

key_terms.meaning: The World Bank's independent mechanism, created by the Board in 1993.
Management's response to a finding of non-compliance.
The party a complaint is made against, here the lender.
The lender's own standard on harm to people and the environment.
An organisation that helps affected people reach a mechanism.

worked_example.title: Route a complaint
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A transmission line has senior debt from one development bank, a partial risk guarantee from another, equity from a bilateral fund and loans from domestic banks. Harm comes from the land clearing.
steps: Find which financier supported the land-clearing component, from the appraisal or procurement notices.
That institution's mechanism has jurisdiction, so read its eligibility rules and time limits.
Use the safeguard framework in force when the project was approved.
Pair the filing with domestic routes, since only they can order remedies.
worked_example.answer: File with the mechanism of the financier of the harmful component, and pursue domestic remedies alongside.

mistakes: Using today's safeguard framework when the project was approved under an earlier one.
Expecting a mechanism to order compensation or stop work.
Waiting until harm has crystallised before establishing who financed the project.

recall.q: When did the Inspection Panel begin operating?
recall.a: 1 August 1994.

recall.q: Who does the Inspection Panel report to?
recall.a: The Board, and never management, which is the source of its independence.

recall.q: Name two things a mechanism cannot do.
recall.a: Order compensation, halt a project directly, or bind the borrower government.

recall.q: Which mechanism covers IFC and MIGA?
recall.a: The Compliance Advisor Ombudsman.

recall.q: In India, which route has the teeth?
recall.a: The domestic route. The lender mechanism is valuable for the record it creates and the influence that record gives.

sections.title: Following the money in practice
sections.big_idea: Split 'who is financing this project?' into four questions and answer the hard one: **who carries the downside**.
in_plain_words: Lender, terms and builder are usually easy to find, while the downside needs the concession agreement and its schedules. Follow six steps in order: name the project, find the approving authority, get the appraisal, get the agreements, map the parties and check compliance. Each step supplies the identifiers the next one needs.

Work the sources in order of yield, from MDB project pages and clearance portals down to RTI requests, which are sharpest when sent last. Date everything and keep the document itself, since a summary can be wrong. **If you cannot answer the risk question from public documents, that is itself a finding** you can report.

diagram.caption: four questions with four different sources

key_terms.meaning: The ministry, department or board that signed off the project.
The rationale, design, expected results and risks of a project.
A procurement notice naming the winner and price, which persists online.
A right to information request for what other sources did not disclose.
The date you saved a document, which keeps research citable.

worked_example.title: Match each question to a source
worked_example.setup: You are tracing a road PPP near you. Pick a source for each of the four questions.
steps: Who is lending: the appraisal document or project signage.
On what terms: the loan or financing agreement.
Who builds and operates: the procurement award and company filings.
Who carries the downside: the concession agreement and its schedules, which may need an RTI request.
worked_example.answer: Appraisal, financing agreement, procurement award, and the concession agreement with its schedules.

mistakes: Starting in the middle of a controversy, which leaves documents about a project you cannot identify.
Sending an RTI request first, when a sharper one follows the other sources.
Citing a URL without saving the document and its retrieval date.

recall.q: Which of the four questions is the hardest?
recall.a: Who carries the downside.

recall.q: Name the six steps of a trace.
recall.a: Name the project, find the approving authority, get the appraisal, get the agreements, map the parties, check compliance.

recall.q: Why do award notices matter?
recall.a: They persist online even when tender documents are withdrawn.

recall.q: Why save the PDF?
recall.a: Sites reorganise and pages are withdrawn, so a saved copy with a date outlasts a URL.

recall.q: What does an unanswered risk question count as?
recall.a: A finding, and a reportable one.

sections.title: What to check before you cite
sections.big_idea: A number without its year is **a rumour with a decimal point**, so run five questions before using any figure.
in_plain_words: Different parts of the deck age at different speeds. Statutory thresholds change over years, climate finance totals change annually with a two to three year lag, safeguard frameworks every few years, and monetisation figures annually. Check each against the source the table names.

Ask five questions of any number: what year, who published, counted how, compared to what, still current. For Indian figures, add whether the number is for the Union or for the general government, because **a Union figure quoted as national can understate the total severalfold**. The deck closes with six points to keep and the one question to ask repeatedly.

diagram.caption: five checks before any number is used

key_terms.meaning: The year a figure describes, to be stated with the number.
What would have happened without the intervention.
A national-government figure that excludes state spending.
Union and state spending taken together.
A claim that survives checks on year, publisher, method and comparison.

worked_example.title: Vet a climate claim
worked_example.setup: A pamphlet says developed countries gave US$115.9 billion of climate finance and calls it grants. Apply the five questions.
steps: What year? The deck gives 2022, and reporting lags by two to three years.
Who published? Developed countries, reporting on themselves.
Counted how? At face value, so loans count like grants; the assessed range is US$28 to 35 billion.
Compared to what, and still current? Set it against the stated need and check revisions.
worked_example.answer: The claim fails on method: it counts loans at face value, so it overstates what was given.

mistakes: Quoting a Union figure as a national one where states do most of the spending.
Trusting an institution's own report as an independent source.
Using a figure with no year attached.

recall.q: What are the five questions before using a number?
recall.a: What year, who published, counted how, compared to what, and still current.

recall.q: What is the sixth question for Indian figures?
recall.a: Is the number for the Union or for the general government?

recall.q: Where should safeguard frameworks be checked?
recall.a: The version in force when the project was approved.

recall.q: How fast do climate finance totals change?
recall.a: Annually, with a two to three year lag.

recall.q: Which one question does the deck end on?
recall.a: Ask who carries the downside, and keep asking until someone shows you the clause.

sections.title: Lenders and cases the map leaves out
sections.big_idea: Export credit, other bilateral lenders, debt distress and municipal finance all need the same habit: **work from the documents, and name what is unknown**.
in_plain_words: Export credit agencies finance their own country's exporters, so tying and weak complaint routes are typical. Bilateral lenders outside the traditional donors disclose less, so trace them from the borrower's side. Debt distress moves from a rising burden to rollover trouble, arrears and restructuring, and capital budgets are cut first.

Municipal bonds stay with a few cities because creditworthiness follows own revenue. Guarantees form a loop when the state counter-guarantees an MDB. Outcome-based instruments make the indicator a financing term. Remittances, FDI and portfolio flows behave differently in a crisis. **Procurement decides who actually receives the money.**

diagram.caption: cases the deck adds after the main modules

key_terms.meaning: A state-backed body that finances or insures its own exporters.
Cover for default caused by specified government non-performance.
The state's promise to indemnify the guarantor.
An outcome instrument that pays investors on verified results.
Funding linked, formally or in effect, to buying from the lender's country.

worked_example.title: Trace a guarantee loop
worked_example.setup: An MDB issues a partial risk guarantee for a power project, and the borrowing state counter-guarantees it.
steps: The guarantee appears to move the risk off the public balance sheet, to the MDB.
The counter-guarantee makes the state indemnify the MDB if the guarantee is called.
So the risk travels back to the public balance sheet by a second document.
Ask where the risk finally rests after every instrument in the chain.
worked_example.answer: The risk rests with the state, because the counter-guarantee returns it by a second document.

mistakes: Assuming aid is the largest external flow. For many countries it is not.
Filling a gap in lender disclosure with assumed terms.
Reading a guarantee as a line when it is a loop through counter-guarantees.

recall.q: Why do export credit agencies matter for infrastructure?
recall.a: A power plant or metro is an export order from the lender's point of view, and they move very large sums.

recall.q: Which spending is cut first in a debt problem?
recall.a: Capital spending, before salaries and transfers.

recall.q: Why is restructuring harder than it used to be?
recall.a: Creditors now include non-Paris Club official lenders, dispersed bondholders and collateralised debt.

recall.q: Which flow reverses fastest in a crisis?
recall.a: Portfolio investment.

recall.q: Name two ways procurement rules get weakened.
recall.a: Specifications written for one supplier, and splitting contracts to stay under a competitive threshold.

notes.2: Use the agenda to see the shape of the argument. Modules one to three teach the vocabulary, four and five explain the turn to private capital and project finance, and six to nine cover India, land, climate and complaints. Ten and eleven teach method, and twelve fills the gaps. Return to the slide ranges to find one topic.
notes.4: Both numbers are honest, and they answer different questions. US$115.9 billion counts loans at face value, while US$28 to 35 billion nets out repayment and interest. Whenever two finance figures clash, stop arguing about the facts and ask what each one counts. That habit is the whole course.
notes.5: Use the scope list to avoid hunting in the wrong place. This course covers money from outside a country's budget and the institutions around it. Budget mechanics, rents and CSR sit in other ImpactMojo courses, which the slide names. Reading a concession agreement is a different skill from reading a Union Budget.
notes.6: Find your audience on this slide, then read the two lists at the bottom. They say what you will be able to do, such as reading a loan's concessionality and locating statutory documents, and what you will be unable to do, such as pricing a bond. Check any figure's source year before using it.
notes.7: Learn these four definitions exactly, because the rest of the course leans on them. The favourable terms define development finance. Mobilisation hangs on the word caused: capital that would have come anyway is only accompanied. De-risking means the public side absorbs risk through guarantees, offtake commitments or revenue floors.
notes.8: Run the same US$100 million through the table. A grant has a grant element of 100 per cent and adds no debt. A near-market loan adds to the stock and to annual service. A guarantee costs nothing until it is called. The headlines look identical, and the fiscal consequences differ.
notes.9: Memorise the three questions: who bears the risk, who repays and when, and what was given up to get it. Reporting usually skips the third, yet a tariff formula or procurement rule conceded in the deal is part of the price. Look for answers in the loan agreement, concession agreement or appraisal.
notes.10: Read the table as four eras, each with a different idea of what blocks development: capital, policy, institutions, and finally too little public money. Each left something behind. Safeguards and complaint mechanisms come from project lending, conditionality debates from adjustment, and all now operate in a system built around the fourth row.
notes.11: Compare the two columns to see why the old vocabulary no longer covers everything. A bank lending to a state faces a government borrower and a loan agreement. A de-risked private project involves an SPV, clause-by-clause risk allocation and fragmented records. The central question moves from conditionality to who carries the downside.
notes.12: These five points are the course in miniature, so keep them as a checklist for any finance story. Read the closing caution as the tone of the course. Development finance can do good, and nobody here is accused of bad faith. The claim is narrower: the form money takes has consequences that headline size hides.
notes.14: Sort lenders by who owns them and who they lend to. The row to remember is the private arm of an MDB. Its borrower is a company, the safeguard regime differs and the complaint mechanism is a different body. That changes where you would file a complaint.
notes.15: Voting follows capital, with a small equal allocation of basic votes. Read both lists before drawing conclusions. Large shareholders hold structural influence, yet the slide warns against assuming the biggest shareholder dictates every decision, since staff, borrowers and consensus reached before the Board all shape outcomes.
notes.16: Spot the tension in the Articles. The Bank may not interfere in political affairs, yet safeguards and governance loans are political in effect. You need not resolve it. Remember it because it explains why safeguards are written as technical standards instead of as rights.
notes.17: Treat IBRD and IDA as two terms sheets from the same bank. IBRD lends near market terms to middle-income countries, and IDA gives grants or credits with long grace to the poorest. Moving from IDA to IBRD is a large fiscal event, so eligibility thresholds are a live political question.
notes.18: Sort the claims about AIIB and the NDB into assumed and tested. The slide lists four tests: speed, safeguards, effect on incumbents and complaint cases. Its last line is the one to carry: competitive pressure on standards is an empirical claim, so test it before repeating it.
notes.19: The finding is that reform of conditionality is largely presentational. The count of conditions changed more than their reach, and social protection appeared more in framing than in binding requirements. Notice why the claim can be disputed: the coding scheme is published, so anyone can recheck it.
notes.20: Learn this method, the most portable technique in the module. Obtain the documents, code each condition by policy area, separate binding conditions from stated intentions, and count. Apply it to loan covenants or concession schedules to turn a rhetorical dispute into a countable one.
notes.21: Outcomes come from three actors together: staff, the board and domestic coalitions. A campaign aimed only at the lender hits one of three. Note the reverse case too, where a government uses an external condition as political cover and exports the blame. That helps explain why conditionality persists.
notes.22: Use this as revision, then read the closing paragraph for the point beneath it: institutional detail is where the politics happens. Voting weights, the political-prohibition clause and IDA terms each decide whose preferences prevail. Campaign without knowing which body decides what, and you will aim at the wrong target.
notes.24: Read across each row to find who is on the hook and when money moves. The sovereign loan and the guarantee look alike in public debate but behave differently: one moves on disbursement, the other only on a trigger. Mixing those two rows causes most of the confusion.
notes.25: Check the six commercial terms in order: principal, interest, maturity, grace, fees and currency. Currency is the quiet one. A hard-currency loan serviced from rupee revenue puts exchange risk on the borrower, outside the interest rate. Ask what currency the project earns in and who absorbs the mismatch.
notes.26: Plot debt service year by year before judging a loan. A long grace period flatters the early years, which is the span a political cycle covers, and the peak may land on a later administration. The same logic applies to a thirty-year concession, which binds officials who will have left.
notes.27: Governments like guarantees because no cash leaves the treasury on signing. Auditors worry because the liability is real, unpriced and correlated, so several may be called together. The useful question on the slide is what has to happen for a guarantee to be called, and what else goes wrong then.
notes.28: Compare the three lending types by where disputes arise. Investment loans bring disputes on procurement and displacement, policy loans on whether a condition was met, and results loans on whether a result is real. In results-based lending the MEL practitioner becomes party to a financing dispute, because a weak indicator misdirects money.
notes.29: Concessionality can be computed. The grant element is the face value minus the present value of repayments, shown as a percentage of face value. Everything hangs on the discount rate: a higher rate raises measured concessionality, so a generous rate inflates reported concessional finance. That is why the standard is contested.
notes.30: Use debt sustainability analysis to structure a conversation about repayment, and treat its output as a projection. The result depends on assumptions about growth, exchange rates and interest rates over long horizons, and those assumptions are choices. A contingent liability that nobody quantified does not become zero.
notes.31: Use this table as a document hunting list. The concession agreement matters most and is hardest to obtain, because risk allocation lives there and its schedules carry obligations the main text only gestures at. Request appraisal documents and procurement awards first, since they are often published.
notes.32: Treat the closing paragraph as the habit to keep: ask the currency question. If a project earns rupees and services dollars, no clause in the loan lists that as a risk, and a twenty per cent move in the exchange rate can turn comfortable debt service into an impossible one. Ask what currency the revenue and the debt are in.
notes.34: The 2015 argument is easy to follow: the SDGs need far more than aid budgets can supply, so public money should mobilise private capital at a multiple. The arithmetic is accepted. The dispute is whether the mechanism delivers the multiple and what policy it costs to try.
notes.35: Read the Cascade as a decision order: first ask if the private sector can finance it, then what reform would let it, and only then use public money. The detail to catch is the burden of proof. Public financing becomes the residual, which is either prudent stewardship or a structural bias.
notes.36: Gabor reads three policy documents as one project: escorting institutional investors into a new asset class. In her account the state absorbs demand and political risk. Her consequence is lost policy space, with particular concern for a just transition that may need tariff changes or asset retirement.
notes.37: Teach a critique fairly by separating what it establishes from what stays open. The documents are public and de-risking does transfer specified risks, so those points stand. Whether mobilisation ratios are poor, how large the policy-space loss is in practice, and whether the argument fits a state like India remain open.
notes.38: Mobilisation is the testable claim, so look at the data. The OECD publishes amounts mobilised by instrument, sector and recipient income group. The cut to watch is income group, which is politically significant. Remember that attribution is itself a standard: who gets credit for a private dollar is a convention.
notes.39: Ask two questions of any mobilisation figure. Additionality: would the investment have happened anyway? Attribution: when several instruments precede one investment, who gets the credit? Reporting standards answer by convention, so find out which convention produced a number before comparing two totals.
notes.40: Look at where mobilised money lands: more in middle-income than low-income countries, and more in energy, banking and industry than in health or education. The cause is structural, since private capital needs a return and social sectors often lack revenue. Ask what the mechanism should be expected to do at all.
notes.41: Blended finance mixes concessional and commercial money, often with the public tranche taking first loss. Use the two question sets as an appraisal checklist. The design questions ask how much concession is the minimum and who captures the upside. The disclosure questions ask whether terms, counterfactual and failures are public.
notes.42: The summary says both sides describe the same mechanism accurately and disagree about the counterfactual. Supporters point to small aid budgets, and critics to risk transfer and lost policy room. Evidence on additionality would settle it and is thin, so treat confident claims in either direction with scepticism.
notes.44: Project finance lends to a single project, usually in an SPV, and looks to its own cash flows. Because the sponsor's exposure is capped at its equity, the legal counterparty may be a thin company. Identifying the right respondent is the first task in any complaint.
notes.45: Use this table to name the parties in any project and what each wants. Everyone in the first seven rows has a negotiated position. Affected people, in the last row, have no contract, and their position comes from statute and the safeguard regime. Keep that asymmetry in mind when you read the deal.
notes.46: Risk allocation is the whole document, so read the table row by row and note how each risk is shifted: fixed-price contracts, liquidated damages, take-or-pay, hedging, swaps. The row with the biggest effect on public policy is political and regulatory change, where a change-in-law clause can require the state to compensate.
notes.47: Both instruments move demand risk off the investor. Under an availability payment the state pays for keeping the asset available, whatever its use. Under take-or-pay the offtaker pays for a contracted quantity whether or not it takes delivery. Ask whether the price of that transfer is known and disclosed.
notes.48: The financial model is the real document: a spreadsheet whose terms are set to produce an acceptable equity return. Ask for its key assumptions. The demand forecast, discount rate and operating cost usually show whether the deal is generous. Small changes in demand can shift the tariff a lot.
notes.49: Optimistic demand forecasts are the most documented pathology in infrastructure appraisal. The incentive is the problem: the forecaster works for the promoter and nobody checks outturn. Use the reviewer's list: who produced and paid for the forecast, the last three outturns, penalties for over-forecasting, and whether a range was given.
notes.50: Expect renegotiation, because nobody can foresee three decades. The Kelkar Committee argued it should be designed for. Without a pre-agreed framework, renegotiation happens under duress with unequal information, and the state must choose between a bad deal and a stalled asset.
notes.51: Read in this order: appraisal, concession agreement, environmental and social assessment, procurement award, implementation report. Each answers one question: what it is for, who carries the risk, who lives there, who builds it and what actually happened. The slide says the sequence takes a day.
notes.52: The key idea in the summary is that a concession differs in kind from a procurement. A procurement buys a thing, while a concession allocates an uncertain future between parties. A summary shows what the drafter was comfortable summarising, so go to the risk allocation table and the schedules.
notes.54: Read the table as a sequence. India wound down its development financial institutions in the 1990s and 2000s, banks then lent heavily to infrastructure and many loans became stressed, and NaBFID in 2021 reverses that judgement. Whether it works depends on the bond market the first attempt lacked.
notes.55: NaBFID shows the de-risking argument written into law. Authorised share capital is Rs 1,00,000 crore, in 10,000 crore shares of Rs 10 each, and the shareholder list runs from the Central Government to pension funds. Its mandate also includes developing bond and derivatives markets.
notes.56: The case for a DFI is the maturity mismatch: banks fund themselves with short-term deposits while infrastructure loans run fifteen to twenty-five years. A DFI can fund long through bonds, if a long-tenor bond market exists. That is why the Act gives NaBFID a market-development mandate too. Judge it on both.
notes.57: The pipeline identified Rs 6 lakh crore of monetisation potential over FY2021-22 to FY2024-25. The mechanism is a contractual partnership: ownership stays public, and the right to operate and collect revenue passes for a period. Government reporting put realised monetisation at about Rs 3.85 lakh crore over three years.
notes.58: Monetisation trades future revenue for present cash, and the valuation question is the whole question. Weigh the case for (no construction risk, capital recycled, ownership retained) against the questions to examine. Above all, find the discount rate used to value the future stream and check whether it is disclosed.
notes.59: Viability gap funding is a capital grant for a project that is desirable and yet commercially unviable at a tariff users can bear. Use the two lists as a test. It is defensible when competitively bid, capped and disclosed, and suspect when negotiated, based on the promoter's own forecast, or stacked on a demand guarantee.
notes.60: Use Kelkar's recommendations as a checklist to trace, finding out for each what was implemented. The diagnosis was that contracts were drafted around fiscal transfer instead of service delivery and that disputes had nowhere sensible to go. The gap between a good report and its implementation is itself the subject.
notes.61: Use this table to choose a source for each question. Two are underused: parliamentary answers, often the only public figure for a project, and CAG reports, slow but backed by statutory access to records. To see which safeguards survived committee, compare a Bill as introduced with the Act as assented, using PRS.
notes.62: Compare three routes to the same road. They differ less in what gets built than in who carries the downside and which document you must read. Budget works carry cost-overrun risk, PPP concessions carry demand guarantee and change-in-law risk, and monetised assets carry the risk of under-valuing the stream sold.
notes.63: The summary offers two threads. India has tried most available models, each adopted partly because the last disappointed, which should make you cautious about the current one's permanence. And the disappointments were about forecasting, risk allocation and renegotiation, which are execution questions that follow whichever model is chosen.
notes.65: Two statutes carry the weight in India: the land acquisition Act of 2013 and the EIA Notification of 2006. A finance course covers them because they generate the documents that describe a project's social and environmental cost, often the only description available to anyone outside the project.
notes.66: The 2013 Act changed process as much as substance: social impact assessment, consent for certain acquisitions, and entitlements in the statute itself. Read the closing paragraph for the key point. Affected families include the landless, such as labourers and artisans, and that provision is the most often under-implemented.
notes.67: Follow the five steps: notification, social impact assessment, public hearing, expert appraisal, and award with rehabilitation. The assessment identifies affected families as well as landowners. For an organisation supporting affected people, the Act's schedules are the operative part, because a project cannot contract below a statutory floor.
notes.68: Learn the five EIA stages and what each produces. Screening decides category A, appraised centrally, or category B, appraised by the state, so it decides the forum. Draft reports are published before the hearing, so the window to respond is narrow and known. Hearing minutes put objections formally on file.
notes.69: Clearance conditions are the terms on which a project was permitted, so they are enforceable. The slide gives a routine: list the conditions, find the measurable ones, request the compliance reports and compare them with the ground. Non-compliance is a factual question, which makes this a tractable route.
notes.70: Keep the two consent standards apart. The 2013 Act's consent is a procedural requirement with a numerical threshold. Free, prior and informed consent is an international and lender standard. Where both apply, ask which standard binds which party. Disputes about consent often turn on the survey that decides who counts as affected.
notes.71: Look for the exemptions, because that is where the disputes are. The recurring ones are category boundaries, expansions riding on earlier clearances, urgency provisions, and project splitting. Splitting means appraising one development as several smaller projects so each stays under a threshold the whole would cross.
notes.72: Take away three things. The two statutes make projects describe their own cost. The 2013 Act sets a floor that contracts cannot go below. Compliance with a promoter's own clearance conditions is the most tractable challenge. No legal training is needed, only knowing the documents exist and asking for them.
notes.74: Climate finance totals are built from choices, and the table lists five. Every row is a defensible convention and each moves the total up. That consistent direction is the pattern to notice. It explains how US$115.9 billion and US$28 to 35 billion can coexist without anyone falsifying a number.
notes.75: Keep three questions apart: adequacy, direction and predictability. A total can grow while the adaptation share falls, so direction is where the distributional consequences sit. Predictability matters to the officials who must spend the money, because a ministry cannot build a multi-year adaptation programme on a flow it cannot forecast.
notes.76: Adaptation lacks a revenue stream. A sea wall or early warning system produces avoided losses, and avoided loss is no return to an investor. So mitigation attracts blended and mobilised finance more readily, and adaptation depends on grants and public budgets. The cause lies in the instrument, and effort has little to do with it.
notes.77: Learn the three categories: mitigation, adaptation, and loss and damage. The third is contested because it is closer to compensation, which implies responsibility. For South Asia, slow-onset losses such as saline land fit no existing window, so how eligibility is drafted decides whether they can be funded at all.
notes.78: Read the four publishers in a deliberate order: the treaty body's assessment first, because it is candid about definitions, then the OECD series, then the shadow report that recalculates the same data. The best exercise in the module is reading the OECD series and the shadow report side by side for one year.
notes.79: Replace the word greenwashing with five checkable practices: relabelling, over-attribution, double counting, instrument inflation and definitional drift. Each can be tested against published methodology. Before you accuse anyone, say which practice you allege. An accusation that names none is not yet an argument.
notes.80: Read India's NDC and long-term strategy for their financing paragraphs. Look for the stated cost of the transition, how much is expected domestically, what is asked of international climate finance and what conditions attach. Then set the stated requirement against the delivered flows on the earlier slides, and do the arithmetic yourself.
notes.81: Apply four questions to any climate finance claim: what year, grant or loan, whose money, counted how. Reporting lags two to three years, and the instrument alone can change an answer by a factor of three. Apply the checklist to friendly sources too, so you find a weak number before an opponent does.
notes.82: The summary stresses that the gap between reported and assessed climate finance comes from conventions, with no falsification. The closing caution says these problems do not make climate finance a fiction. The fair reading is that every common convention raises the total, so read the figures as negotiated figures.
notes.84: The Inspection Panel was the first independent accountability mechanism at an international financial institution, created in September 1993 and operating from August 1994. Its independence comes from reporting to the Board. Remember its limit: it assesses compliance with the Bank's own policies and cannot award compensation.
notes.85: Sort the two lists into what a finding gives you and what it cannot. It can produce a public finding and an action plan, and it creates a record other forums can use. It cannot compensate, halt a project or bind the borrower government, because the respondent is the lender.
notes.86: Identify which institution financed the specific component that caused harm, because that decides the mechanism and the safeguard policy. The table maps institutions to mechanisms. Remember the complication: large projects have several financiers with different standards, and harm from the whole project may fit no single mechanism neatly.
notes.87: Follow the five-step sequence: identify the financier, find the policy breached, establish harm and link, file, and follow the action plan. The catch is the policy version: the framework in force at approval binds the project, and today's version may differ. Read eligibility criteria and time limits before filing.
notes.88: Most eligible complaints are never filed, and the reasons are practical: people do not know who financed the project, documents are in English and online, time limits run, and fear of retaliation is real. The intermediary list shows how an organisation can close that gap, from identifying the financier early to advising on time limits.
notes.89: Read two or three case files end to end, including the action plan. A finding with a weak plan and no monitoring is a document and no remedy. Read a case the mechanism declined to take up too, since eligibility decisions show where the boundaries are drawn and how to draft a future complaint.
notes.90: Use domestic and lender routes together. Indian forums can order remedies and MDB mechanisms cannot, but MDB mechanisms can find fault with the lender, which domestic forums usually cannot reach. The slide's conclusion: for most Indian projects the domestic route has the teeth, and the lender route leaves the record.
notes.91: The summary gives the system in one line each and ends on a balanced verdict. The mechanisms were a real innovation and have changed designs, yet they are slow, cannot compensate and are reached mostly by people with an intermediary. Hold both halves before deciding to spend months on a filing.
notes.93: Split the question of who is financing a project into four. Lender, builder and terms are usually easy, an afternoon's work. The fourth, who carries the downside, needs the concession agreement and is the one worth the effort. Know in advance which documents are normally published and which are claimed as confidential.
notes.94: Follow the six steps in order, because each supplies identifiers for the next. The official project name opens the clearance portal, the approving authority tells you whose records to request, and the appraisal names the parties. Starting in the middle leaves a folder about a project you cannot conclusively identify.
notes.95: Work down the table in order of yield. MDB project pages and clearance portals give the most, procurement award notices persist after tenders expire, CAG reports are slow but citable, and parliamentary questions sometimes hold the only public number. Keep RTI for last, when you know the exact gap.
notes.96: Adopt two habits that cost only minutes. Date every note, because thresholds and institutional names change. Keep the document, and skip the summary: save the PDF with its retrieval date, since pages get moved or withdrawn and a dead URL is worth far less than a saved copy.
notes.97: Do the exercise on a real project near you and write a sourced answer to every question. The final question is the test: if demand disappoints, who absorbs the loss? If you cannot answer it from public documents, that is itself a finding you can report.
notes.98: The summary frames tracing as a means to an end. Split the question, follow six steps, work the sources in order, and date and save everything. The aim is one paragraph, with sources, stating what the project commits the public to and what it owes affected people. That paragraph must survive being checked.
notes.100: Expect this deck to age at different speeds. Thresholds and rules change over years, climate totals annually with a two to three year lag, and monetisation figures annually. Use the table to find where to recheck each kind of figure. As the slide says, a number without its year is a rumour with a decimal point.
notes.101: Run five questions on any number: what year, who published, counted how, compared to what, still current. For Indian figures add the sixth: Union or general government? Union figures exclude state spending, so quoting one as national can understate the total severalfold where states do most of the spending.
notes.102: Choose a next step by purpose. The Deep Dive offers 26 annotated readings that include everything cited here, so take it to go deeper on evidence. Public Finance and Political Economy cover the domestic and institutional side, and the Studio and Explorer tools help you trace funds in practice.
notes.103: These six points compress the course, and the last line is the one to keep: ask who carries the downside and keep asking until someone shows you the clause. Use the other five as your revision list, and check each against a project you know.
notes.105: Export credit agencies finance their own country's exporters, so a power plant is an export order from their side. Check the tying arrangement, the standards applied and whether any complaint route exists. If a project's equipment all comes from one country, look for an agency behind it: terms may be good while competition is absent.
notes.106: Bilateral lenders outside the traditional donor group often disclose less, with confidentiality clauses over terms. Work from the borrower's side: budget documents, audit reports, parliamentary answers and the state's own debt reporting. Treat a missing agreement as a finding to report, and say what is unknown without inferring terms.
notes.107: Debt distress comes in stages: rising service burden, rollover difficulty, arrears, restructuring. Capital budgets are cut before salaries and transfers, so the first visible sign is often a stalled construction site, with no announced austerity programme in sight. Use the table to place a country and predict what gets cut.
notes.108: Restructuring is harder now because creditors are more varied: official bilateral lenders outside the Paris Club, dispersed bondholders and collateralised debt. Coordination failure is the binding problem, since each creditor class waits for the others to take losses. The debtor stays in limbo, and limbo is expensive.
notes.109: Indian urban infrastructure depends on bodies with weak own revenue, and creditworthiness follows own revenue. That is why bond issuance stays with a handful of cities. Note the closing point: own revenue is a political question about property tax. The instruments tried include pooled finance and land-based financing.
notes.110: Read guarantee types as a loop. The fourth row is the one to catch: when an MDB issues a partial risk guarantee and the state counter-guarantees it, the risk that seemed to leave the public balance sheet returns by a second document. Ask where the risk finally rests.
notes.111: Outcome-based instruments pay on verified results, with the investor bearing delivery risk. The recurring problems are high transaction costs, gameable metrics and few independent evaluations. The last line is for MEL practitioners: the indicator is chosen at contract stage by people who will be paid on it, so a weak one moves money wrongly.
notes.112: Compare the five flows by how they behave in a crisis. Remittances have held up or risen when a receiving economy weakens, while portfolio flows reverse fastest. A resilience plan built on the wrong row fails when it is needed, so avoid assuming that aid is the largest flow.
notes.113: Procurement decides who receives the money, and it matters most for local effect and corruption risk. Learn the five weakening tactics: tailored specifications, exclusionary thresholds, single-source awards, contract splitting and post-award variations. Award notices persist online after tenders are withdrawn, so they are the easiest document to obtain.
notes.114: Use this glossary to check your own definitions. Notice the terms that depend on each other: the offtaker's creditworthiness decides financeability, availability payments place demand risk on the payer, and a change-in-law clause compensates the private party. Write each in your own words and test it against a real contract.
notes.115: Treat these three open questions as invitations. Does de-risking produce more real investment than the alternatives? Do accountability mechanisms change outcomes? Is a DFI the right vehicle for Indian infrastructure? The deck leaves them open on purpose, so form your own view from the sources and change it when the documents say otherwise.
